content: Psychological therapy and counseling for patients with mental health disorders and/or substance use comorbidities have been shown to significantly increase the initiation and completion of hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment. These interventions also lead to higher sustained virologic response (SVR) rates, indicating improved treatment outcomes. Integrating services for specific populations, such as people who inject drugs (PWID), may further enhance the effectiveness of HCV care. The Guidelines Development Group reviewed evidence from recent systematic reviews on interventions aimed at improving linkage to care following HIV testing. This evidence was deemed relevant to hepatitis care and treatment services. The feasibility, acceptability, and resource use of such interventions were also considered, including education and support for peer and lay health-care workers. Findings consistently demonstrate that lay health workers can effectively perform a variety of interventions typically carried out by trained medical personnel. This approach strengthens service delivery capacity in diverse clinical settings, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Lay health workers are critical in supporting the decentralization of services and non-facility-based testing. Peer-led interventions have been shown to be both feasible and acceptable to the individuals being screened and to the lay health workers themselves. The low-cost nature of these interventions makes them particularly suitable for resource-limited settings. In studies reviewed, lay health workers received training to tailor educational interventions. This training was relatively simple and cost-effective. Clinician reminders, which align with broader efforts to standardize clinical practice, have also proven effective. These reminders facilitate provider-initiated screening and systems-based approaches to improving clinical outcomes. Implementation of such systems is relatively straightforward, and similar approaches have demonstrated success in other disease modalities, such as breast and colorectal cancer screening. Integrating HCV screening and treatment with mental health and substance use services has been shown to be both feasible and acceptable to targeted clients. Chapter 17 of the referenced guidelines provides examples of integrated care models in various settings that promote linkage to hepatitis care. While the interventions addressing multidisciplinary or integrated care were diverse, a key factor contributing to improved outcomes was the co-location and coordination of services. Cost and cost-effectiveness data were not reported in the systematic review. However, effective linkage to hepatitis care and treatment following a positive diagnosis is expected to improve program effectiveness. This includes supporting earlier treatment initiation and reducing loss to follow-up before treatment begins, potentially resulting in cost savings across the care continuum. Proactive linkage approaches are essential components of comprehensive hepatitis testing services. Countries should establish specific policies and strategies to improve and prioritize linkages between hepatitis testing, prevention, treatment, and care services. Interventions that impact multiple steps along the care continuum are generally more resource-efficient. The effectiveness of linkage strategies may vary depending on the testing approach used. Linkage to prevention services is particularly important for individuals at high ongoing risk, such as PWID and serodiscordant couples. Monitoring and evaluation of linkage following hepatitis testing are critical to strengthening treatment and prevention cascades. Success should be measured by enrollment in care rather than intermediary process indicators, such as the number of referrals issued. Without strategies to ensure linkage and enrollment in care, the full impact of hepatitis testing on reducing HBV or HCV transmission, morbidity, and mortality cannot be realized. There is a significant need for methodologically rigorous studies to evaluate the effectiveness, costs, and cost-effectiveness of various intervention packages and combinations. These studies should aim to optimize engagement, retention, and treatment outcomes for individuals living with HBV and HCV, particularly in LMICs. Efficient coordination of testing services at the national level is crucial for an effective and sustainable hepatitis testing program. National testing policies should outline goals, objectives, and responsibilities for testing services at each level of the tiered testing network. These policies should align with broader national health policies and address the needs of key populations, including those in prisons and other closed settings. Strategic planning for testing services requires a situation analysis to map existing facilities and assess their capacity, infrastructure, technical and human resources, and financing. A minimum package of testing services should be agreed upon for each level of the health-care system, including community-level services. National regulatory mechanisms should oversee the activities of the viral hepatitis testing program, including pre-market and post-market controls for in vitro diagnostics (IVDs), certification of testing staff, and accreditation of testing services. An effective oversight system builds confidence in testing services among stakeholders. For countries lacking regulatory capacity, the WHO prequalification assessment can provide independent evaluations of the quality, safety, and performance of IVDs intended for use in resource-limited settings. A national reference laboratory with relevant expertise and experience should be designated to oversee quality control, organize quality assessment schemes, and provide training and supervisory support. Building or expanding capacity for viral hepatitis testing services should be integrated into broader efforts to expand access to testing for related diseases. This includes developing a trained and motivated health workforce capable of addressing co-infections, such as HIV/HCV. Human resource management should ensure that all testing staff are appropriately trained, certified, and proficient in their roles. Supervisory support and regular site visits should be part of a quality assessment system to provide feedback and address challenges. Reliable procurement and supply chain systems are essential to ensure the continuity of test kits, reagents, and consumables. Testing services should have systems in place to monitor stock levels, expiration dates, and consumption patterns to prevent stock-outs and wastage. Testing kits and reagents must be transported and stored under controlled conditions as specified by the manufacturer. Proper storage and maintenance of equipment, including calibration and preventive maintenance, should be planned as part of financial and procurement procedures. Laboratory information management systems should minimize transcription errors, protect patient confidentiality, and ensure the quality and integrity of test results.
